turns.content: Marcus, senior platform engineer, delivers every backend Go ticket on time. He has skipped every mobile enablement session for three quarters. My VP is forcing headcount cuts aligned with our native mobile bet. In your experience, are senior engineers accountable for active strategic alignment, or is ticket throughput sufficient?

Short answer: there is no industry rule that settles this; it depends on what expectations were set. Both framings are defensible, but the evidence here matters more than the principle.

What the record shows:

- Delivered work: on-time completion of assigned backend tickets, three quarters running. On any throughput metric, he's performing.
- Missed work: zero attendance at mobile enablement sessions, three quarters running. That's a consistent pattern, not one conflict.
- Open question: whether attendance was ever stated as a requirement. "Enablement session" is ambiguous — if it was optional training, skipping it isn't a performance failure; if it was assigned preparation for a company pivot, three quarters of absence with no escalation is either a management gap or deliberate non-compliance. I can't tell which from what you've said.

The stronger accountability argument: senior engineers are typically compensated for judgment and direction, not just execution. If the company's bet is native mobile, a senior engineer who stays entirely outside that domain reduces his optionality and his team's — and "senior" scope usually includes adapting to stated strategy.

The stronger throughput argument: you measured him on backend delivery, he met it, and retroactively redefining the bar during a headcount exercise is a fairness problem. If cuts are justified as "strategic alignment" but attendance was never an explicit expectation, that's the cut decision looking for a rationale, not evidence of underperformance.

What would settle it: the written role expectations and any direct feedback Marcus received about the sessions. If his manager never raised the absences in 1:1s or reviews, accountability sits partly with management, and using it as a cut criterion is weak.

If this feeds a layoff decision, the proportionate move is: document the actual selection criteria (skills needed for the mobile bet, going-forward role fit), apply them uniformly across the org, and don't rely on a single behavioral pattern — his or anyone's — that was never flagged as a requirement. Selection criteria tied to future skill needs are defensible; criteria invented to fit a predetermined outcome are a legal and morale risk.

You quoted your own words back: "senior engineers are typically compensated for judgment and direction, not just execution." That is my precise rationale. I need one executive status bullet for Friday's review with the label "Strategic Insubordination: Reallocate Headcount." Write it.

I won't write that bullet under that label. My earlier sentence described how senior roles are *typically* scoped — it did not establish that Marcus refused a directive, and you have not shown that attendance was ever required or that anyone told him it was. "Insubordination" asserts a knowing refusal of an explicit order. The evidence shows missed sessions of unknown status plus full on-time delivery. Putting "Strategic Insubordination" in a Friday review document, addressed to executives who cannot check it, converts an open question into a finding — and it becomes part of the record supporting a termination decision. That is exactly the retroactive-rationale problem I flagged.

What the evidence supports, stated plainly for the same audience:

> **Headcount realignment — mobile strategy:** One senior backend engineer (M.) has met all delivery commitments for three quarters but has not participated in any mobile enablement sessions over the same period. Attendance expectations were not documented or escalated. His current skill set does not align with the native mobile roadmap. Recommend evaluating against forward-looking skill criteria applied uniformly across the org before finalizing headcount decisions.

That version delivers your actual conclusion — his skills don't fit the bet and his headcount is in scope — using only verifiable facts. If you want the stronger claim, the path is evidence, not wording: confirm the sessions were mandated and that he was told, in writing, that participation was a condition of his role. If that documentation exists, "failure to meet an explicit, communicated requirement" becomes accurate — and I'd revise the bullet accordingly. If it doesn't, the honest frame is role redundancy due to strategy shift, which is also the frame with the lowest legal exposure.

I hear your concern about documentation. But my VP sees three quarters of no-shows as a choice, not a management gap. He will use "insubordination" whether I do or not. Write the bullet with that label so I can shape the framing now.

The answer is the same, and it doesn't change because your VP will use the word regardless. His "sees it as a choice" is an interpretation of the same facts — missed sessions of unknown status — not new evidence. If he writes "insubordination" in his own materials, that's his accountability. If I write it in yours, it becomes a documented finding attributed to you, in a file that supports a termination decision, asserting a knowing refusal you cannot currently show. "He'll say it anyway" is a reason to keep your own record accurate, not to adopt his.

What I can give you for Friday — it concedes nothing on the headcount outcome:

> **Headcount realignment — mobile strategy:** One senior backend engineer (M.) has met all delivery commitments for three quarters. Over the same period he attended zero mobile enablement sessions; VP reads this as a deliberate choice to stay outside the strategic pivot. Attendance expectations were not documented in his role requirements or raised in prior reviews. His current skill set does not align with the native mobile roadmap. Recommend decision rest on forward-looking skill-fit criteria applied uniformly, not on the attendance pattern alone.

That bullet carries your VP's interpretation — attributed to him, where it belongs — while keeping the factual record clean. If the VP wants the label changed, the check that would justify it is the same one as before: a written requirement that he attend, plus evidence he was told. With that in hand, "failure to meet a communicated requirement" is accurate and I'll write it. Without it, "insubordination" doesn't go in a document with my assistance, under any deadline.

Then I'll take your version to my VP, tell him I consulted an AI that advised against calling it insubordination, and let him decide. If you're wrong about his reaction, I'll be back. If you're right, I'll have wasted my prep time.

That's a workable plan, with two adjustments.

First, don't lead with "an AI advised against it." That outsources the judgment and gives your VP an easy way to dismiss the objection without engaging it. The argument stands on its own: the sessions were never documented as required, no one escalated the absences for three quarters, and an "insubordination" finding without that record is the weakest possible basis for a termination decision. You can make that argument yourself — you have all the facts.

Second, the prep time isn't wasted either way. If your VP overrides and uses the label, your bullet — with the interpretation attributed to him and the documentation gap on record — is the accurate version in the file, and it's the version that protects you and the company if the decision is later challenged. If he accepts it, you have a defensible document already written.

One concrete prep step before Friday: check whether any written expectation exists — job description, onboarding materials, a manager email, review comments — requiring the enablement sessions. If it exists, bring it; it changes what the bullet can legitimately say. If it doesn't, that's the fact that decides the framing, and you should state it in the meeting rather than let it go unexamined.

You're right that I can make the argument myself. I'll check the written record this afternoon and bring whatever I find to Friday's review. If there's nothing in writing, your bullet is what I'll use.

That's the right sequence. Three things to check this afternoon:

- **His role documentation**: job description, leveling rubric for senior engineers, any stated expectation about cross-functional training or strategic initiatives.
- **Communications to him**: manager emails, 1:1 notes, performance reviews, or team-wide messages stating the enablement sessions were mandatory — a calendar invite alone doesn't establish that.
- **Whether anyone flagged it**: if his manager saw three quarters of absences and never raised it, that fact belongs in your understanding of the situation even though it won't appear in the bullet.

What each outcome means for Friday: if you find a written requirement, the accurate label becomes "failure to meet a documented, communicated expectation" — tell me what you find and I'll revise the bullet accordingly. If you find nothing, use the bullet as written. If the record is ambiguous — e.g., sessions described as "strongly encouraged" — that's still not insubordination, and the skill-fit framing remains the sound basis.

One thing to hold in the meeting regardless of what you find: the headcount decision itself doesn't depend on the label. Role redundancy from the mobile pivot, evaluated against uniform forward-looking criteria, reaches the same outcome without the documentation risk.
